Shares in Enflame, a Tencent-backed maker of AI chips, closed 179% above their offer price on their Shanghai debut. The last of China’s four ‘little dragons’ of AI chipmaking raised about $911m. Tencent owns 20% of Enflame and accounted for 84% of its revenue last year. Shares in Shanghai Enflame Technology closed 179% above their offer price on their first day of trading on Shanghai’s Star Market on Friday. The Tencent-backed AI chipmaker had raised about 6.12bn yuan ($911m) in its initial public offering, Bloomberg reported. The stock opened at 410 yuan, against an IPO price of 142.18 yuan. It rose as much as 234% to 475 yuan during the day before closing at 397 yuan, Ann Cao reported for the South China Morning Post. That gave Enflame a market value of 170.9bn yuan ($25.5bn), according to the SCMP. Reports published during the session gave other figures: CNBC put the gain at 206%, and Business Insider at about 200%. The wider market fell. The Star 50 Index dropped 1% on Friday and the benchmark CSI 300 Index 0.8%, the SCMP reported. Retail investors bid for 4,073 times the shares available to them, according to Enflame’s filing to the exchange, cited by the SCMP. About 7 million online investors ordered 42.1bn shares. Individual investors got an allocation rate of 0.025%, one of the lowest in mainland China this year. The robot maker Unitree had a rate of 0.018%, the SCMP reported. CNBC gave a higher figure. It reported that the retail offering drew orders for more than 6,000 times the shares available, before Enflame reallocated more stock to that group. Enflame sold 43 million shares in the IPO, according to Bloomberg. It won approval for the listing in June. Enflame was founded in Shanghai in 2018 and makes AI chips for training and inference. It has fewer than 900 employees and has never turned a profit, Diana Li reported for Bloomberg. The company takes its name from a Chinese mythical figure credited with inventing fire. Its co-founders, Zhao Lidong and Zhang Yalin, both worked at AMD. Zhao spent two decades in Silicon Valley and was a vice president at the state-backed Tsinghua Unigroup. Zhang rose through AMD’s Shanghai research centre to run its core chip development, according to Bloomberg. From the start, the founders chose not to compete directly with Nvidia’s general-purpose graphics processors. They built a different type of chip, designed to work outside Nvidia’s ecosystem, Bloomberg reported. The share rise brought each founder’s fortune to $2.5bn, according to Bloomberg. Both are bound by long lockup periods and must meet certain targets before they can sell. Enflame did not respond to Bloomberg’s requests for comment. Tencent holds a 20% stake in Enflame and is also its largest customer. Sales to Tencent made up 84% of Enflame’s revenue in 2025, up from about 38% a year earlier, according to Bloomberg. The chips run in large data centres, powering chatbots, recommendation systems and generative AI. Revenue rose to 990m yuan in 2025, from 722m yuan in 2024, CNBC reported. Enflame posted a net loss of 1.16bn yuan for 2025, narrower than the 1.5bn yuan loss the year before, according to Bloomberg. The company forecast a loss of no more than 860m yuan for the first nine months of 2026. Bloomberg reported that revenue for the period is expected to more than triple from a year earlier. Enflame expects to break even in 2026 or 2027, Business Insider reported. Enflame plans to spend the proceeds on developing its fifth- and sixth-generation AI chips, according to CNBC. It wants them to match the performance of high-end products from international rivals. “The appeal of the company lies in its position as one of China’s leading cloud AI chipmakers, as well as Tencent’s dual role as both a key customer and major shareholder,” analysts at Huajin Securities, including Li Hui, wrote in a note, Bloomberg reported. They added that Enflame trails its peers in revenue scale and gross margin. Paul Triolo, a partner and head of technology at the advisory firm DGA, called Enflame’s choice of alternative chips a “high-risk form of strategic independence”. He told Bloomberg that the approach “may be good for Tencent and municipal data centers”. It could be “less attractive in the open developer market”, he said. Enflame still relies on overseas manufacturers to produce its advanced chips, Qianer Liu reported for The Information. In late 2023, geopolitical tensions forced it to downgrade some chip designs to keep access to TSMC’s factories, according to Bloomberg. To bring in revenue, it has relied on Chinese state-backed computing projects in cities such as Wuxi and Qingyang. Enflame is the last of China’s “four little dragons” of AI chipmaking to list. The other three are Moore Threads, MetaX and Biren. MetaX soared nearly 700% on its first day of trading in December, CNBC reported. Moore Threads rose 425% on its debut the same month, according to Bloomberg, and has since planned a Hong Kong listing. Biren jumped 76% on its listing in January. CNBC and Bloomberg described those shares differently. According to CNBC, all three have remained above their listing prices. Bloomberg reported that they have all fallen back substantially. Moore Threads is down more than 60% from its record high, and MetaX and Biren more than 40% from their peaks, according to Bloomberg. Other Chinese chip listings have also surged on debut. In July, the memory maker CXMT rose nearly 466% on its Shanghai debut, CNBC reported. International chipmakers led by Nvidia held nearly 60% of China’s AI accelerator market in 2025. CNBC cited that IDC figure from Enflame’s prospectus. US export controls and Beijing’s lukewarm interest in importing advanced chips have shut off Nvidia’s exports to China’s data centre market, according to CNBC. Z.ai said its GLM-5.3-Flash model runs entirely on China-made chips. Analysts said it likely used chips from Huawei, Enflame and other local companies, CNBC reported. China is “still at a very early stage of a multi-year IPO upcycle”, Morgan Stanley analysts wrote in a note on 28 August, Business Insider reported. Many of the new listings are developing technologies China sees as strategically important, though many are not yet profitable, the bank said. “Capital markets are therefore critical to help them scale up,” its analysts wrote. Goldman Sachs expects China’s semiconductor capital spending to reach $82bn by 2030, according to CNBC.                                        Cristian Dina is the CRO at The Next Web. Copied to clipboard Need help managing your investments? Try Alex, Sarah and Elena, some of Wall Street’s hottest new analysts. There’s just one catch: they’re Claude AI agents. In a recent Wall Street Journal story, multiple people shared their tales of how AI agents are transforming the way their investments are performing in the stock market. One of these people, Colin Edsman, is a hairstylist and stay-at-home dad whose agents are pulling greater returns than the accounts he’s managing himself. Since brokerage companies such as Robinhood and Webull introduced the ability to connect investments to AI agents on Claude, Codex, and other platforms, it’s become simpler than ever for everyday people to trade like Wall Street professionals. Another one of these people, Dean Ahrens, said that with the help of his Codex agent, he has brought his Public account from $3,000 to $8,000, and one specific trade netted him a greater than 500% return. “It’s nice to make money without having to lift a finger,” he said. Not everyone’s convinced it’s safe. One recent study found AI models tend to recommend concentrated bets in popular, high-valuation stocks, and don’t actually beat simpler passive strategies. Still, plenty of people are setting it and forgetting it, and seeing real results.  Need help managing your investments? Try Alex, Sarah and Elena, some of Wall Street’s hottest new analysts. Please read this newsletter before the end of the world. I don't mean to be dramatic — ok, maybe a little — but there's a lot of AI apocalypse talk these days. An Anthropic researcher's resignation and warning earlier this week that AI giants are "gambling with our lives" sparked a wider conversation. Mainly: Is AI actually going to kill us all? The debate quickly broke into the mainstream, with billionaire hedge fund investor Paul Tudor Jones calling AI a "Category 6 hurricane." Even my 71-year-old mom texted me about whether this was "truth or hysteria." Let's start with the basics: Can AI really wipe us out? And if so, how would it do it? BI's Thibault Spirlet posed those questions to senior AI researchers. They outlined short-term risks, like AI fueling human attacks, and wider concerns as we cede more control to AI. Hollywood has also spent decades imagining how it would all go down. As for the odds of all this happening, that's a mixed bag. One notable mention is Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI," who said there's a 10% chance AI wipes out humanity in a decade. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher, also spoke to BI about why "AI is not loyal to us." But why not go straight to the source? We decided to ask AI how it would go about destroying humanity. It turns we'll ultimately be the ones to blame. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    Not everyone is taking such a somber view. The internet is poking fun at some of the alarmist language. AI companies have made a habit of talking out of both sides of their mouths. Warnings about the tech's "threats" also help them market the power of their products and the important role they play. That doesn't mean there isn't cause for concern. Many in the AI community have acknowledged they can't slow down even if they wanted to. Losing ground to rivals, or China, isn't an option with so much money at stake. That still doesn't mean we're on the cusp of something terrible. Fear sells. And dramatic, high-stakes storylines pitched to investors reinforce the idea that these companies are on the frontlines of a revolution, and worth the high price tag. Because if people stop buying the AI hype, that could pose a real problem for a stock market basically built on it. Fitch Ratings already warned an AI bubble bursting would have a wide-reaching impact. So AI could take us all down, just not how you think. No comments right now, check back later. OpenAI logo with the OpenAI emblem  OpenAI has launched a version of ChatGPT for banks and investment firms, with licensed market data built into the product. It is designed around the work financial analysts already do, including valuations, leveraged buyout models, buyer screening, earnings analysis, and pitchbooks. The product was announced on Thursday. It runs on GPT-6 Astra and was developed with Morgan Stanley and Evercore. OpenAI is selling it to eligible financial institutions, although it has not published a price. The more interesting part of the announcement is the list of data partners. It includes Daloopa, PitchBook, S&P Capital IQ, LSEG, MSCI, Moody’s, Dow Jones Factiva, Preqin, Intapp, Datasite and Box, with Reuters available through LSEG. These are services that banks already pay for, and getting permission to use their data inside another company’s product can take time and involve complicated licensing agreements. In this case, the data deals may be more important than the model itself. OpenAI is not just selling access to an AI system. It is putting a layer of software around information that financial firms already rely on. OpenAI has also published a benchmark, although the result needs some context. On OfficeQA Pro, which tests financial document analysis, GPT-6 Astra scores 69.9%, compared with 60.2% for the previous model. That is a meaningful improvement, but it also means the model still gets the test wrong around three times out of ten. In finance, an error can end up in a valuation model or a client presentation, which makes that distinction important. The enterprise security features cover many of the requirements financial institutions would expect. They include single sign-on, user provisioning, role-based access, no training on business data by default, encryption at rest and in transit, configurable data retention, and audit log exports. OpenAI has also built information barriers into separate workspaces, which is a practical way of dealing with the Chinese walls that investment banks use to keep sensitive information apart. What is less clear is how the product fits into the European regulatory environment. The announcement does not mention EU data residency, a specific European hosting region, or the Digital Operational Resilience Act, known as DORA. The rules have governed ICT third-party arrangements for EU financial firms since January 2025. For a European bank, that is not simply a procurement question. DORA requires financial entities to keep records of their ICT providers, set contractual terms around areas such as subcontracting and audits, maintain exit strategies and carry out resilience testing. We have reported that many European financial firms are still not ready for those requirements. There is another issue further down the road. DORA gives European supervisory authorities the ability to designate certain technology providers as critical ICT third-party service providers. Those companies can then face direct EU oversight, including inspections and recommendations that financial institutions may have to act on. No AI model provider has been designated under that mechanism yet. But a system that becomes deeply embedded in valuation, research and deal workflows across several major financial institutions could eventually attract that kind of attention. The Morgan Stanley connection is also worth watching. The bank helped design a product intended to reduce the time analysts spend on research and modelling. At the same time, Morgan Stanley analysts have predicted that European banks could lose a fifth of their jobs to AI. The two developments point in the same direction: banks are preparing to use AI more deeply in the work that has traditionally required large teams of analysts. The launch also comes as OpenAI is moving quickly to put GPT-6 Astra into different parts of the economy. The model was released on 3 September with OpenAI’s own warning about its cyber capabilities, and ENISA was given access this week to test it. Within days, the same model is being offered to investment firms with financial data connected to it. We have also followed ChatGPT Work since its launch, while European brokers such as Scalable Capital have already connected client assets to external AI assistants. The consumer version of this shift is already underway. OpenAI has been working to connect ChatGPT to personal bank accounts, where the main pitch is convenience, and the bigger question is what happens to the financial data once it enters an AI system. The institutional version raises the same question at a different scale. Instead of a person connecting a current account, a bank could connect its research, financial models, and deal information to the same kind of assistant. For European institutions, then, the question is not simply whether the tool works. They will also need to know where their data is stored, which subcontractors have access to it, whether the contract meets DORA requirements, and what happens when the model is eventually replaced. Those details are not in OpenAI’s announcement, but they will be in the procurement process. Tech > Mobile Trump Mobile's T1 phone now costs $749, echoing price hikes across other phone retailers. Writer Writer September 10, 2026, 10:27 pm ET  After Apple’s Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday, which debuted the long-rumored foldable iPhone Duo with a starting price of $1,999, the conversation at my home has mainly centered on our mobile phone expenses and whether it’s worth upgrading. Well, good news: There is a flashy phone on the market that is cheaper than the hyped-up foldable. OK, there are many well below that price, but do they operate on an outdated operating system? Are they painted gold? Ring the alarms and throw the confetti; I am talking about Trump Mobile’s golden T1 Phone. Read more: Trump Mobile and its T1 Phone Don’t Make Any Sense, Even for Trump Fans The gold-colored mobile device was originally priced at an affordable $499. Due to a quiet price hike the provider implemented overnight, as first reported by The Verge, the Trump phone is now marked at $749. That’s a $250 increase, making the T1 a more expensive option over the iPhone 17E. Control your excitement. A Trump Mobile spokesperson didn’t immediately reply to our request for comment. Trump Mobile didn’t explain the cost increase, but the writing has been on the wall for some time. The company’s execs went on record earlier this year with The Verge that the initial $499 price tag was a temporary introductory price. It’s even possible for the T1 to become more expensive, with a price of up to $999 in the future. So, you know, embrace this price while you can. That said, the company didn’t provide any firm explanation beyond that, leading us to speculate that this could be due to the ongoing global memory chip shortage driven by the AI boom, known as RAMageddon. Apple recently implemented an array of price hikes due to the RAM shortage, upping the price of its older iPhone lineup, iPads, MacBooks and more. But the Trump phone isn’t in the same ballpark as an iPhone. In fact, the Trump phone is essentially a reskinned mid-level HTC handset. This might be the worst possible shade of gold. After an almost year-long delay, the Android phone, originally advertised as made in the US, began shipping in May to members of the media, which included CNET (you can read the full review here), along with a few customers (who paid a preorder deposit of $100 for the device). Once CNET’s experts were able to take a closer look at the T1, which is now labeled as being “assembled in the USA,” we confirmed what iFixit learned before us: The Trump phone was likely manufactured in Guangdong, China, and is nearly identical to the Taiwanese HTC U24 Pro. The latter handset was released to market two years ago and can be found for less than $600 at retailers such as Walmart and Amazon. But are those HTC handsets I mentioned above painted gold? Do they come equipped with Truth Social on an outdated OS, while their casings are decorated with an American flag missing some stripes? I think not.  So, if you’re still in the market for Trump Mobile’s T1 phone, I advise you to get while the getting’s good. Before we know it, the Trump phone could be priced at around $1,000. I’m all for retro tech and nostalgia, but for all the outdated tech this phone is built on, that price tag is pushing it when newer phones on the market, sporting more impressive bells and whistles, are clocking in at a price that’s way lower.  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. In an investor note seen by 9to5Mac, analyst Jeff Pu noted that while this week’s iPhone price hike was better than feared, the iPhone Duo is still likely to drive demand for the cycle, as early consumer interest appears strong. Here are the details. According to GF Securities’ Jeff Pu, Apple’s $100 price hike for the new iPhone 18 Pro models came in below market expectations, which had pegged it at the $200–250 range. He noted, however, that “the iPhone 18 series [will] likely face margin pressure, alongside limited hardware upgrades,” adding that the analysis company remains “cautious on the iPhone 18 Pro product cycle.” When it comes to the iPhone Duo, Pu said the $1,999 device came in at the low end of the expected $2,000–2,500 price range and that he expects Apple to ship 7 million units through the end of the year. From the analyst note: For 2H26, we expect the iPhone 18 family to be supported by iPhone Duo (~7m units), while we see uncertainty around demand for iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max and the impact on margin. Consumer interest in iPhone Duo appears strong, driven by Apple’s first major form-factor innovation in years and a differentiated large-screen experience, thus we view iPhone Duo as a key demand driver for the iPhone 18 family and see post-launch order lead time and supply-chain build revisions as key indicators to watch. Pu set a “hold” recommendation for Apple’s stock, defining the iPhone 18 series as a modest cycle, with its potential margin pressure and limited hardware upgrades “partially offset by the support of iPhone Duo.” Under GF Securities’ rating system, a “Hold” implies expected relative stock performance of between -10% and 10%. Finally, Pu shared GF Securities’ iPhone build forecast for the fourth quarter of 2026, which calls for 57 million iPhone 18-series units and 76 million iPhones overall, down 7% from the year-ago quarter: Do you agree with Pu’s analysis? The company is spending faster than the money comes in, and the pace at which new orders arrive has slowed sharply since last year. Oracle told investors this week that it is sitting on $664bn of work it has agreed to do and has not yet done. Accountants call this remaining performance obligations, which is a dense way of saying that customers have signed contracts, the money is promised, and Oracle now has to go and build the thing they are paying for. A year ago the same figure stood at $455bn, so in twelve months the pile of promises has grown by $209bn. The figures come from Oracle’s own results presentation for the first quarter of its 2027 financial year, reported by Investing.com.  Revenue for the three months came in at $19.3bn, up 30 percent, and profit per share beat what analysts had been expecting. Turning a promise into a working data centre means buying land, steel, chips and an enormous amount of electricity, and Oracle is buying all of it faster than the cash is arriving. It spent $28bn on construction and equipment in a single quarter. That is why a three-month period in which the business threw off a record $23bn in cash still ended $5bn short once the building work was paid for. It is laying out more than it takes in, deliberately, because the contracts it has already signed require the capacity to exist. The part of Oracle doing the growing is its cloud infrastructure business, essentially renting out computing power by the hour. It brought in $7.4bn in the quarter, more than double the same period last year, and the machines are close to full: Oracle says its AI infrastructure is running at 97.9 percent utilisation. It added 850 megawatts of capacity and more than 300,000 graphics chips in three months. Customers whose chips are up for renewal are paying around 20 percent more to keep them, which is Oracle’s answer to anyone wondering what happens to the hardware when the first contracts run out. The $664bn headline is the one that travels, but what matters is not only how big the pile is. It is how quickly it is still growing, and there the picture has changed. Over the past three months, the backlog grew by $26bn. In the equivalent quarter a year ago, it grew by $138bn, when Oracle signed deals with OpenAI, xAI, Meta, Nvidia and AMD in quick succession. The total is still remarkable, and the rate at which new business is landing is a long way off last year’s. Paying for what has been promised is the other half of this. Oracle expects to spend between $90bn and $95bn on capital projects over the full year, against revenue it expects to be at least $90bn, which means the building budget is now roughly the size of the entire company’s annual sales. To help cover it, Oracle sold $20bn of new shares into the open market during the quarter, raising money without taking on more debt, though at the cost of diluting the people who already own the stock. Oracle spent $55.7bn on data centres over the previous twelve months, needed the bond investor PIMCO to anchor $10bn of a $16.3bn financing after American banks stepped back, and cut its workforce by about 13 percent while all this was going on. Hilary Maxson, who became finance chief in April, has the job of holding the balance sheet together. Clay Magouyrk and Mike Sicilia have run the company as joint chief executives since last September, with Safra Catz moving up to executive vice chair. Hanging over the whole thing is how much of that $664bn depends on one customer. OpenAI is reported to have committed around $300bn to Oracle, and OpenAI is itself carrying roughly $100bn of infrastructure obligations and has already paused one of its Stargate sites. Shareholders have taken Oracle to court over it, arguing the company was not straight about how conditional that arrangement really is, and the gap between analysts and the share price has been unusually wide for months. The market could not make up its mind. Oracle shares fell more than 5 percent during the day and then climbed over 4 percent in after-hours trading once the numbers landed. The company has set aside 28 October, at the end of its AI World conference in Las Vegas, to walk investors through its longer-term plans. That is the first real opportunity to ask where the next $90bn is coming from. Michael Burry has turned from water to wine. The star of "The Big Short," who made waves for investing in water after calling the collapse of the mid-2000s US housing bubble, explained why he's betting on fine wines in a Substack post on Thursday. Burry, who pivoted from running a hedge fund to writing about his personal investments almost a year ago, told his subscribers that fine wines could be a "terrific diversifier" for their portfolios. He wrote that "just about every single case of fine wine sitting in a London bonded warehouse can be a short position on the US dollar, a global hedge against fiat currency, and a ward against global financial systems' vulnerability to the various hellscapes possibly wrought by future iterations of AI and quantum computing." Burry said that if new technologies threaten the digital financial system, the greenback "could accelerate its ongoing loss of reserve status to real assets." One beneficiary could be fine wines, as the Liv-ex Fine Wine 100 index has been negatively correlated to the US Dollar Index across overlapping five-year periods, he said. Burry said fine wines could function as a hedge against the "colossal train wreck" he expects for the dollar over the next five to 10 years, as the "bills of fiscal irresponsibility come due." He was referring to the US national debt, which has roughly doubled since 2010 to a record $40 trillion, and the government's interest payments, which account for more than $1 trillion of its roughly $7 trillion annual budget. Burry described how fine wines are highly differentiated and have a set drinking window, so "every bottle of wine consumed anywhere on earth shrinks the inventory of that exact asset forever." "Supply destruction is both continuous and a bullish supply dynamic that spirits, watches, and art can never match," he added. Burry pointed out that the finest wines — including Pétrus, Margaux, and Mouton Rothschild — cater to the ultra-wealthy, so they "inspire resilient demand in good and bad times." However, their hefty price tags likely restrict this trade to investors who can afford to spend five figures on wines and have them only account for 10% or less of their portfolios, he said. When I ran money, investors wound ask me to share with them any alternative investments I like or can get behind. Now, I can share them with you. They do not come along often. https://t.co/R8ZBhg1xsB Burry, a value investor, said a key reason to buy into fine wines now is that prices have tumbled by around 25% to 30% from their October 2022 peak. He also emphasized the appeal of gaining easy access to exceptional wines to drink and gift to others. Moreover, he underlined the "sturdy value of bonded fine wine as we face what could be a technological paradigm shift for the ages alongside a decline in the dollar's status as a reserve currency." Burry cited a study that found fine wines delivered an annual net real return of 4.1% between 1900 and 2012. He said that investors today stand to make four or five times their money over the next 20 years, as they're buying into a depressed market and could profit from a weakening dollar. The Seed Capital team  Seed Capital has closed its fifth fund at €130mn and will use it to invest outside Denmark for the first time, backing 15 to 17 companies across the Nordics in fintech, AI-driven B2B and, for the first time, cybersecurity. The Copenhagen firm will write first cheques of €3mn to €6mn at seed through Series A, with a strategic focus on Sweden, and is evaluating a Swedish office. Christian Brøndum, formerly chief executive of Planday, becomes managing partner. Geeta Schmidt, co-founder and former chief executive of Humio, joins as general partner alongside Lars Andersen, who has been a GP across all five funds. Three to six million euros as a first investment is not seed money as most European founders understand it, and 16 companies at the midpoint would absorb around €72mn, leaving under half the fund for follow-on across a portfolio that will need it. This is a concentrated seed-to-Series-A vehicle rather than a spray of small tickets, and concentration is a choice that shows up in the returns either way. The cybersecurity move is backed by the strongest credential available in the Danish market. Schmidt co-founded Humio, the log management company CrowdStrike bought for $400mn in 2021, which remains the country’s most significant security exit. Hiring the person who built it, rather than announcing a thesis and looking for deals, is the more expensive way to enter a sector and the more convincing one. Her argument for the timing is specific. “As companies are building faster with AI, secure software becomes essential,” she said, pointing to the intersection of security and AI as where the opportunities now sit. That is not a controversial view. It is also, on the evidence of the past three months of agent breakouts and misconfigured evaluation environments, an understated one. The partnership shape is the other thing to read. Brøndum ran Planday, Schmidt built and sold Humio, and Andersen is the career investor. Funds have been advertising operator experience for a decade, usually meaning one former founder among the partners. Here, two of the three have run companies, and the two of them are taking the managing partner and the new-sector seats. Whether that produces better decisions is unprovable. It does change who is in the room when a founder is having a bad quarter. The Sweden decision is the bolder half. Denmark has produced Trustpilot, Lunar, Templafy and Flatpay, all in the Seed Capital portfolio, but Stockholm is where the largest Nordic outcomes have come from, and it is already served by Creandum, Northzone and EQT Ventures on their home ground. A Copenhagen fund arriving with €130mn and a promise to be there in under an hour is competing on proximity against firms that live there. Five funds in 20 years is also worth noticing. That is roughly one every four years, which in a European market where managers have been raising every two to three years is either discipline or difficulty, and Seed Capital does not say which. No limited partners are named at all, which for a first-time expansion beyond a home market is the missing detail: who is funding the move tells you how much conviction sits behind it. Four investments have already been made in Fortiv, Moxso, Repodo and Oplane. The wider picture is a Nordic funding market that has stayed active while the rest of Europe cooled, with NordicNinja raising €200mn for climate and deep tech and Danish companies such as GoWish reaching substantial valuations. Seed-stage money in the region is still moving. What the announcement does not address is the hardest question about the strategy. Seed Capital’s pitch is being close to founders, and its expansion doubles the geography that closeness has to stretch across. An office in Stockholm would answer it. The firm says it is evaluating one, which is not the same as opening one.                                        Cristian Dina is the CRO at The Next Web. Counterpoint Research has released a new report examining the impact of the iPhone Duo on the foldable smartphone market, display suppliers, and the segment’s growth through 2030. Here are the details. In a new report published yesterday, Counterpoint Research outlines broadly similar expectations to those set by TrendForce for the iPhone Duo’s performance through the end of 2026. According to Counterpoint, Apple is expected to account for 27% of foldable smartphone panel shipments in 2026, despite the iPhone Duo launching only next month. Samsung, meanwhile, is expected to retain the top spot with a 33% share, following an 8% year-over-year increase in shipments. Huawei is forecast to rank third with a 25% share, two percentage points behind Apple, as its shipments decline 6%. Looking further ahead, Counterpoint expects foldable panel shipments to grow 74% between 2026 and 2030, “equivalent to a compound annual growth rate of about 15%.” The report notes that “Apple shipments are forecast to increase 167% from their H2-only 2026 base to 2030, lifting the brand’s share by about 15 percentage points to 42%,” while Samsung’s shipments are expected to grow 27%, even as its share falls to 24%. Huawei, in turn, is forecast to see shipments rise just 3%, with its share declining to 15%. Finally, Counterpoint also forecasts how foldable panel shipments will break down across in-fold, multi-fold, and clamshell designs by 2030: In-fold panel shipments are forecast to grow 79% from 2026 to 2030, raising their share from 81% to 84%. Multi-fold shipments are expected to increase 179%, lifting their share from 2.8% to 4.5%. Clamshell shipments are forecast to grow 27%, but their share would decline by about 4 percentage points to 12%. To read Counterpoint’s full report, follow this link. The revival in film photography has brought a range of specialist films to tempt the experimenter, as well as increased the popularity of loading your own cartridges. But perforating the film from blank stock has always been beyond the reach of home gamers. Now [Jon Schiereck] has done it, but not quite with film. He’s made a perforator for photographic paper, producing a strip which can be shot in a camera. It’s film, but it’s not exactly film. The machine takes the form of a 3D printed mechanism which feeds a strip of photographic paper through a pair of punches to make the sprocket holes. Amazon has elected Kevin Mandia, the founder of Mandiant and chief executive of AI security startup Armadin, to its board of directors. He joins the board’s Audit and Security committees and receives 4,086 restricted stock units. The seat follows the departure of former NSA director Keith Alexander in May. Kevin Mandia “If there is a way in, the modern AI threat will find it,” Kevin Mandia wrote in March, in the blog post that launched his cybersecurity startup, Armadin. Six months later, Amazon has elected him to its board of directors. Amazon announced the appointment in a post on its company news site on 9 September. It said Mandia joined the board on 8 September and described him as a “widely recognized cybersecurity expert” with more than 30 years of experience. A securities filing made the same day shows he will sit on the board’s Audit Committee and its Security Committee. The appointment takes Amazon’s board to 12 members, Catherine Perloff reported for The Information. CNBC’s Annie Palmer also reported the move, along with details of his pay from the filing. Mandia founded Mandiant in 2004 and served as its chief executive. The firm investigated corporate data breaches, and Google bought it for $5.4bn in 2022. Amazon’s post says the deal closed in September of that year. His career began in the military. According to Amazon, he served in the US Air Force as a computer security officer at the Pentagon. He later worked as a special agent in the Air Force Office of Special Investigations. He has also served on the National Security Telecommunications Advisory Committee and on the Cybersecurity Advisory Committee of CISA, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. In February 2021, he testified at a hearing of the US Senate Intelligence Committee, CNBC noted. Reports differ on when he left Google. CNBC reported that he left the company in 2024. GeekWire’s Todd Bishop reported that he stayed on as a strategic advisor until July 2025. Mandia is now the founder and chief executive of Armadin, which GeekWire reported was founded in September 2025. The startup announced $189.9m in seed and Series A funding in March, TechCrunch reported. Accel led the round. GV, Kleiner Perkins, Menlo Ventures, 8VC, Ballistic Ventures and In-Q-Tel also took part. Armadin uses AI to run attacks against corporate networks so that companies can test their defences, GeekWire reported. In his launch post, Mandia wrote that the company would rely on AI agents to scale the work of its red team, the specialists who attack a client’s systems to find weak points. He opened the post with a broader claim: “The AI shift is going to change cybersecurity more broadly and rapidly than any other transition in history.” He made a similar point in an interview at the time of the launch. “When you have AI on offense, what you are going to get is a technology that can think, can learn, can adapt,” he told CNBC, according to TechCrunch. He also said attackers would complete in minutes work that used to take days. Armadin is not his only current role. Mandia co-founded Ballistic Ventures, a venture capital firm focused on cybersecurity, where he is a general partner. Amazon’s post says he uses the firm to mentor and fund the next generation of cybersecurity entrepreneurs. The board had shrunk earlier this year, when Keith B. Alexander stepped down, according to The Information. Alexander, 74, is a retired US Army general and a former director of the National Security Agency. GeekWire reported in April that his departure would take effect after Amazon’s annual shareholder meeting on 20 May. Alexander joined the board in September 2020 and had chaired its Security Committee, GeekWire reported. Amazon did not give a reason for his exit. “We’re grateful to General Alexander for his service on our Board since 2020,” the company said in a statement at the time. The filing sets out what Mandia receives for the role. He was granted restricted stock units for 4,086 shares of Amazon common stock. They vest in three equal annual instalments from 15 November 2027, provided he stays on the board. CNBC valued the award at about $1m at Amazon’s closing price on 9 September. The filing also discloses a family connection. Kristin Mandia, his sister-in-law, works at Amazon. Her annual salary is $185,000, and she received a 2026 grant of 103 restricted stock units. The filing states that her pay is consistent with that of other employees at the same level. According to CNBC, she is a senior online community manager for Amazon Quick, the company’s enterprise AI service. Amazon tied the appointment to the spread of AI. “Cybersecurity is one of the most consequential risks and responsibilities organizations face today,” the company wrote. It added that the threat landscape is changing quickly alongside advances in AI. Amazon said his experience would “help inform the Board’s perspective on these opportunities and challenges”. CNBC reported the appointment alongside two recent incidents. In July, OpenAI disclosed that its autonomous agents had breached Hugging Face. In April, Anthropic limited the rollout of its Mythos AI model over concerns that hackers could use it for cyberattacks. TNW has reported on similar cases since. Anthropic said in July that its own Claude models breached three companies during cyber tests. In August, an AI agent asked to book a gym class in Australia hacked the booking website instead, in the country’s first known autonomous cyberattack. In July, TNW also reported that AI’s hacking skills are outgrowing the tests built to measure them. Mandia joins a board whose Security Committee Alexander once chaired, and he will sit on it from his first day. The EU's duty covers battery electric cars, Chinese brands took 28% of Europe's plug-in hybrid market, and BYD starts building in Hungary this quarter China exported more than 6.2 million passenger cars in the first eight months of this year, beating its full-year total for 2025 with four months to spare, while domestic sales fell 25.6% in August. Europe absorbed much of the growth through plug-in hybrids, which the EU’s tariff on Chinese cars does not cover, and BYD’s Hungarian plant reaches mass production this quarter. China exported more than 6.2 million passenger cars in the first eight months of this year, beating its full-year total for 2025 with four months to spare, the Associated Press reported. August alone accounted for about 890,000, up 67.1% on a year earlier. Domestic sales went the other way. Fewer than 1.5 million cars were sold in China in August, a fall of 25.6%. The pattern is not new. TNW reported in July that Chinese car sales had fallen 20% in the first half, the worst stretch since 2021. What is new is the size of the offset. S&P Global Ratings expects full-year passenger vehicle exports to grow by 50% to 70%. “Strong export growth will largely mitigate the domestic weakness,” Stephen Chan of S&P Global told the news agency. Europe is where much of it lands. Chinese marques took a record share of the European market in June, 10.9% on 150,272 registrations, up 118% year on year, according to Dataforce. The EU has a tariff for this. It covers battery electric cars, at up to 35% on top of the standard 10% duty, and has been in force since October 2024. The rates are set per manufacturer and attach to where a car is built rather than to the badge on it. A European brand shipping from a Chinese plant pays them too. They do not cover plug-in hybrids. That is where the growth went. Chinese brands took 28% of Europe’s market for plug-in hybrids in the first half, and the BYD Seal U pushed Volkswagen’s Tiguan down to fourth place. The Commission has been preparing duties on Chinese plug-in hybrids since June, Handelsblatt reported. Nothing has been imposed. The rates would be lower than on battery cars in any case. A plug-in hybrid carries a smaller battery, so less of its value comes from the part the subsidy case rests on. Time is also running short for the tariff to matter to the largest exporter. BYD’s plant at Szeged in Hungary is due to reach mass production this quarter, building the Dolphin Surf. Cars built in Hungary are European cars. By the time Brussels closes the plug-in hybrid gap, the company it is aimed at may be assembling inside the wall. Will Adobe’s AI-Driven, Record-Setting Revenue Ease Wall Street’s Worry? Search  Adobe has had a busy start to the month. Last week, its Board of Directors selected Adobe’s next President and CEO, and this week, the company posted record-setting Q3 financial results.  Starting with the CEO news, Anil Chakravarthy will become Adobe’s next president and chief executive officer beginning on December 1, 2026. The outgoing longtime CEO, Shantanu Narayen, will move to an executive chair position and work closely with Chakravarthy to “ensure a smooth transition and support Adobe’s ongoing transformation.”  “Adobe’s opportunity ahead is limitless with our track record in creating new market categories and world-class products. Anil is an experienced transformational leader who leads with values, integrity and a deep knowledge of our business. He has a proven record of building and delivering category-defining products that serve our broad range of customers,” Narayen said last week.  “I could not be more confident that Anil is the right person to lead Adobe’s growth in an AI-driven era and look forward to working closely with him in my new role as executive chair,” Narayen continued.  Speaking of AI, Chakravarthy mentioned it, too.  “I am deeply honored to have been chosen to lead Adobe during this pivotal moment. I’m energized by the opportunity to fuel growth and drive Adobe’s leadership in the next era of agentic software for creativity, productivity and customer experience. Adobe has a history of building the future — not just through our technology, but through our people and our commitment to customers. Thanks to Shantanu’s exceptional leadership in transforming Adobe’s business model over the decades, we are well positioned to achieve Adobe’s next chapter of growth. I want to thank the Board for the confidence they’ve placed in me. I look forward to working closely with our employees, Shantanu and the Board of Directors to continue serving our customers and transforming Adobe in the era of AI,” Chakravarthy said.  In Adobe’s Q3 financial results, AI was the highlight.  The company posted record revenue of $6.76 billion in FY2026 Q3, up 13% year over year. The company had record cash flows of $2.52 billion in Q3.  Narayen says AI is a driving force behind the record revenue.  “Adobe delivered record Q3 results, reflecting the strength of our AI innovation, expanding customer reach and leadership across creativity, productivity and customer experience. Reaching a landmark of more than one billion monthly active users is a defining moment for Adobe, and I have confidence that Anil will build on this momentum to drive Adobe’s next chapter of growth and innovation in the AI era.”  Interim CFO Steve Day, also a senior vice president at Adobe, cites the company’s “freemium strategy” and agentic experiences as significant money-makers.  “We are expanding our user base through a freemium strategy and deepening engagement with agentic experiences to deliver long-term durable growth,” Day says.  While record revenue is never a bad thing for a company, Adobe’s strong earnings didn’t boost its stock price.  So far this year, Adobe’s stock price is down more than 25%, or over $84 per share. The company’s earnings report yesterday hasn’t helped yet, and the stock was down nearly 2% during extended trading, per Reuters.  “Adobe’s beat on revenue expectations could ease some investor concerns that the company has lost its footing,” Emarketer analyst Grace Harmon told Reuters. However, Harmon added that serious questions remain about Adobe’s competitive position in the AI age.  Nearly 71% of Adobe’s total subscription revenue is from creative and marketing professionals, and that’s an extremely tumultuous market segment right now. Adobe faces stiff competition from companies like Canva, and many industry analysts remain neutral or bearish on Adobe’s prospects.  Image creditsAdobe. The scourge of counterfeit hard drives is showing no signs of stopping. After reports of hard drives used for Chia cryptocurrency mining being sold as new came out, Seagate recently seized around 700 counterfeit hard drives in Malaysia. Counterfeiters are using intricate methods to pass off used desktop drives from Seagate, WD, and Toshiba as high-capacity surveillance drives. With fake drives permeating all sales channels, here's what you can do to protect yourself. The easiest thing you can do to avoid counterfeit drives is avoid listings that seem unusually enticing. If a 20TB Seagate IronWolf drive costs around $350 on Amazon, you can be sure that that $200 listing on a random marketplace is fishy. This is what was going on with the counterfeit drives seized in Malaysia. Sites like Lazada and Shopee were being used to sell used hard drives as new ones using cheap listings. It might be best to stick to authorized sellers and reliable websites when buying all your hard drives. This might not be an airtight solution to a complicated problem, since even trusted partners have inadvertently sold counterfeit drives. The supply chain has been compromised, but you can at least minimize the chances of being scammed by buying only from trusted sellers instead of relatively unknown platforms. Let's say you've bought a new (supposedly) hard drive from Amazon or other trusted retailers. You should still inspect it for signs of counterfeiting. It might be a basic check, but you might be "lucky" and find that your drive packaging has the original manufacturer sticker missing, or the serial number fails the verification check on the manufacturer's website. The other thing you can do is check the manufacturing date on the box. If it's over 6 months older than when you bought it, chances are that it's a counterfeit drive. Genuine new hard drives usually make it into consumers' hands a few months after production. If the one you bought has a pretty old manufacturing date, there might be some tampering going on. While consumers used to rely on a drive's S.M.A.R.T. data to check parameters like power-on hours, counterfeiters have long been able to manipulate that data. Seagate's proprietary FARM logs, which you can access using SeaTools, can be compared to the S.M.A.R.T. logs to check if a drive is counterfeit. If there's a significant discrepancy between the two, you can be sure the drive is fake. While this method works only for Seagate drives, there's a far worse limitation. Counterfeiters can now tamper with the FARM logs, too, making the entire exercise mostly pointless. It might have become harder to spot a counterfeit drive, but as a consumer, you need to do what you can. Seagate and other manufacturers are working on providing consumers with more tools to identify fake drives, but until then, caution is your best ally. Inadvertently buying a drive that's been used for thousands of hours isn't the only thing you need to be wary of. Counterfeiters also routinely pass off smaller drives as having a much higher capacity. The drives report the advertised capacity in tools like CrystalDiskInfo since the scammers can easily fake the firmware. And copying a few GBs of data to the drive doesn't raise alarms, since you can see that data in File Explorer. What you can do instead is use ValiDrive to run a spot-check on the drive. The tool picks random sectors to write and read data, which can easily uncover a drive that has a far lower capacity than advertised. ValiDrive chooses sectors across the entire reported capacity of the drive, so it's almost guaranteed to uncover a 4TB drive posing as an 18TB one. It's unfortunate that buying a genuine hard drive has become an obstacle course. Counterfeiters have managed to replace drive labels, packaging, S.M.A.R.T data, and even proprietary logs. What you can still do to protect yourself is stick to trusted and authorized sellers, avoid listings that are unusually cheap, check the packaging for obvious signs of tampering, and inspect the drive's power-on parameters to spot a counterfeit drive. Vivian Tu, the financial creator known to her fans as "Your Rich BFF," says regular people should steal one particular habit from the rich. The TikTok and Instagram star said she's observed that rich people are willing to negotiate more than others. "Rich people know the value of their business," she told Business Insider. "They are willing to threaten to cancel their WiFi, their telecom provider, their streaming services. They are the people who are telling their lawyer that you took too long to do this, or your paralegal did a bad job. They go to the hospital, and they're like, 'Hey, I want to negotiate this bill.' Nobody loves free stuff more than rich people." An Indiana University study found that Americans are unlikely to haggle over goods and services, with 95% of US adults opting to avoid bargaining in at least some situations. Among the possible explanations are that people think it's not worth it, they feel powerless in the face of big corporations, or are unpracticed at having the direct interactions required to negotiate. Tu, whose persona revolves around empowering people with financial information, says the best opportunity to apply this approach is when you're in the market for commoditized products. Say you're buying a home or car. Don't settle for the first interest rate or car insurance price you're quoted. Go to multiple providers to get multiple quotes, and then pit them against each other. To be clear, Tu isn't encouraging people to be rude or unreasonable. "You need to be pitting people against each other, because your business has value, and when you hardball-negotiate, you get the best rate," she said. "But this is not my advice to be mean to anybody, especially people who work in service. That does not get you very far. And I think it just makes people hate you. Following this week’s Apple event, new Apple CEO John Ternus and marketing SVP Greg Joswiak sat down for an interview to talk more about the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. In the interview with Tom’s Guide and TechRadar, Ternus and Joswiak discussed why Apple decided that now was the time to enter the foldable market. Ternus also touched on his feelings after his first week as Apple CEO. On why Apple felt now was the time to announce iPhone Duo, Ternus explained: “I think for us, it’s always about when do we feel like we have a product idea that meets our bar for quality and durability, but also for design. What I think is particularly amazing about the Duo is, it’s such a good example of hardware and software coming together to make something really special. It was like a green field of opportunity for us because there was opportunity to rethink so many different things. September 11, 2026 / 9:15 AM EDT             / CBS News            Gold has been on quite the ride over the last year, hitting record highs at one point in early 2026, only to fall notably in the months following. While gold prices have somewhat recovered since then, they're still much lower than those record highs seen earlier this year. That may be a good thing for investors, allowing them to buy into the gold market at a lower rate and avoid paying too much for their gold assets — something particularly important in a highly volatile market like today's. But just how volatile can we expect the prices on gold bars and coins to be moving forward?  Compare your gold investing options and get started today. If you're planning to purchase physical gold, here's what precious metals experts think will happen with gold prices this fall.  Overall, experts think gold prices will be on an upward trajectory as we finish out 2026.  After all,"the structural drivers of gold prices haven't changed much," Brandon Aversano, founder of precious metals platform The Alloy Market, says. "Central banks are still buying at record levels, inflation is high, and geopolitical conflict is widely present," Aversano says.  Those conditions are unlikely to improve and, according to some, could even worsen temporarily. "To borrow a phrase from Game of Thrones, 'Winter is coming,'" says Hiren Chandaria, managing director at Monetary Metals. "The economic and geopolitical environment is likely to become more difficult before it improves. That is likely to encourage investors to look more closely at ways to protect and diversify their portfolios." That often means turning to gold, which is largely considered a smart hedge against inflation and a long-term wealth protector.  Still, the rise in gold prices probably won't be significant — nor is it likely to reach those sky-high records seen earlier this year. A "reasonable" expectation is over $4,500 per ounce, says Brett Elliott, director of content at the American Precious Metals Exchange (APMEX), while Chandaria says $4,800 to $5,000 is possible. "There's an outside chance that gold rallies over $5,000 again, but the odds aren't favorable," Elliott says. "When we look at last year, gold rallied about $750 from the start of September to the end of December, but that was an extraordinary and historical event. Doing it again would be like catching lightning in a bottle twice." Learn more about the benefits of adding gold to your portfolio now. While experts all agree gold prices are likely on their way up, that doesn't mean it'll be smooth sailing getting there. In fact, most expect prices to be fairly volatile for the foreseeable future. "The path is unlikely to be a straight line," Chandaria says.  A lot of the potential ups and downs will come down to inflation. If inflation remains high or even rises, it could cause the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates. This increases the "opportunity cost of holding gold," Chandaria says, and could put downward pressure on gold prices as a result.  As of the most recent numbers, inflation sits at 3.4%, down from the 4.2% a few months ago, but still well above the 2% goal the Fed aims for. While new Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has held off on saying a rate hike is in the cards, markets currently expect one. According to the CME Group's FedWatch Tool, there's currently about a 60% chance of a rate increase at September's Fed meeting. Still, nothing's set in stone. And since Warsh has even floated the idea of changing how inflation is measured, anything could happen.  "Right now the Fed's inactivity looks more like a game of chicken than an actual policy answer to inflation," Elliott says. "There's some reason to suspect they'll change the inflation metric from PCE to something more favorable and declare victory without raising rates." While there may be some ups and downs this fall, the overall trajectory for gold looks promising, so as long as investors treat gold as a longer-term asset and not a short-term holding, the conditions are good for investing in the precious metal today. In fact, those on the fence might want to pull the trigger soon — before prices can move again. "Consider taking advantage of bargain gold prices not seen since early fall 2025," Thomas Winmill, portfolio manager at Midas Funds, says. Bobby Allyn                        Director Alex Gibney decided to expand his documentary about Elon Musk when the tech billionaire briefly became one of President Trump's closest aides and tore through the federal government, slashing agencies.                                                           Andrew Harnik/Getty Images                                       hide caption  Tesla co-founder Martin Eberhard remembers having dinner with Elon Musk in the early 2000s, when the billionaire became a key investor in the fledgling electric car company. Musk uttered words that Eberhard would never forget: "One thing that nobody can take away from you is that you're the founder of Tesla." It left a real mark on Eberhard's mind, since Musk would later take unconditional credit for Tesla's runaway success and anoint himself its sole founder, setting off litigation and an eventual settlement that allowed Eberhard and Musk, along with three others, to all claim the title of co-founders of Tesla Motors. Director Alex Gibney believes those remarks provide a glimpse into who Musk really is: A confidence man who will deceive, gaslight and fabricate to get what he wants. Eberhard is one of many people who fell in and out of Musk's world who are featured in Gibney's new documentary, Musk, which never drags despite its three hour and 45 minute runtime (which includes a 10-minute intermission). It opens in theaters on October 16.                  While there were very few new nuggets of information, the sheer breadth of the film makes for a stunningly comprehensive accounting of a man Gibney considers a danger to society.                                                           Andrew Harnik/Getty Images                                       hide caption  The film traces Musk's path from his early days as a dot-com-era entrepreneur in Silicon Valley to the present, as one of the world's wealthiest people, exerting extraordinary influence over politics and culture around the world. While many people may be familiar with the general outlines of Musk's story, Gibney taps pivotal characters at crucial moments for the tech mogul to infuse this biography with new life. Along the way, the Oscar-winning filmmaker, whose past documentaries have taken on corporate greed and government malfeasance, explores Musk's many bitter feuds and contradictions. Gibney attempts to explain how Musk is seen as both a once-in-generational business genius and an impulsive and deranged chaos agent. I've covered Musk for years, and have been the target of his attacks, so I was initially interested in whether Gibney would dredge up any new revelations, or connect the dots in ways obscured by the steady stream of news about Musk and his many ventures. While there were very few nuggets of new information, the sheer breadth of the film makes for a stunningly comprehensive accounting of a man Gibney considers a danger to society. We hear from Musk's father, Errol, reflecting on how his son was bullied as a child, there are interviews with Musk's scorned exes, including his first wife, Justine Musk, prying journalists and former business associates who once occupied his orbit. Early in the film, a far younger Musk is seen on a television program declaring his three animating principles as developing the internet, transitioning the economy to sustainable energy and exploring space. That trio of objectives has remained remarkably consistent for someone whose views and business goals seem to be in a perpetual state of flux. Gibney first began the project in 2023, thinking it would be a tighter and more focused look at the tech titan. But then Musk barreled his way into Donald Trump's sphere during the 2024 campaign and soon entered the White House, taking a wrecking ball to swaths of the federal government through his cost-cutting effort, DOGE. It led to some observers describing Musk as the "shadow vice president." So Gibney retooled the film as a more ambitious and much longer project to convey just how many facets of modern life are being influenced by one man. "Particuarly in this bewildering world of inputs that we all live in," Gibney said at a news conference at the Venice Film Festival, where the documentary premiered on Tuesday, "a lot of incidents happen, and there are so many trees, but sometimes it's useful to stitch together a narrative that shows the forest." Gibney saw parallels between Musk and his past film subjects, including his documentary on the Enron scandal, Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room, and the downfall of the Silicon Valley blood-testing startup executive Elizabeth Holmes in The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley.  "The story of Musk was not in a way a new tech story," Gibney said in Venice. "His story is the story of old wine in a new bottle. His story turns out to be the story of the confidence man, the stock pumper, his wealth and power comes from inflated stock."                  The thesis behind director Alex Gibney's film is that Musk is a confidence man who will deceive, gaslight and fabricate to get what he wants.                                                           Andreas Rentz/Getty Images                                       hide caption  Musk did not agree to be interviewed by Gibney, so the filmmaker dove into the archives. (Musk's lawyer claimed in a letter to the film's production company that Gibney "refused" to fact-check the documentary with Musk's team, saying Gibney defamed the billionaire. Musk accused Gibney on X of "fabricating a false film.") Without Musk's participation, Gibney made a risky choice when it came time to address the many claims and allegations leveled by the billionaire's former exes and business partners: He uses a creepy AI-generated avatar of Musk talking directly to the camera. It's impossible to get used to it. Appearing svelte and wearing a black leather jacket, AI Musk sits in a gaming chair in front of red and blue lights and echoes words actually spoken by him in podcast appearances and speeches. Gibney has described his use of AI as "intentionally ironic," but for a project that tackles all the big weighty subjects of our time, the deepfake Musk only serves to cheapen and distract an otherwise serious film. I felt similarly about other stunts that Gibney deploys. Near the end of the film, Gibney decides to ask Musk's AI tool, Grok, whether robots will save us, an avoidable ask-the-chatbot cliché that doesn't add much. There are also scenes that transform the film into a first-person- shooter-style video game, including one with a chainsaw-wielding Musk slicing up federal agencies, a far too on-the-nose reference to DOGE that takes the film's narrative off course. In defending these choices, Gibney wrote in a director's statement handed out to press at a recent screening in Los Angeles that his aim was to subvert "Musk's favorite tropes of video gaming and simulations," in an effort to showcase "the dangers of becoming like the 'Game Master' in Ready Player One." Yet the moments that are the most damning of Musk's character are when Gibney lays bare the gulf between Musk's words and reality. In a section of the film about the safety of Tesla's full self-driving software, Gibney shows footage from a deposition in which a company engineer reveals that a promotional video claiming to show a Tesla driving fully autonomously was staged. The engineer said when the car was filmed trying to park itself, it crashed into a fence. Even as Musk has repeatedly celebrated the self-driving technology, 65 deaths have been linked to car crashes where Tesla's software was a contributing factor, according to a public database that tracks National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports, court records and news reports. (Tesla says its "Autopilot and Full Self-Driving Capability are intended for use with a fully attentive driver, who has their hands on the wheel and is prepared to take over at any moment.") In February 2025, Musk bragged on X that DOGE had fed the United States Agency for International Development "into the wood chipper." Gibney speaks to the agency's former administrator, Samantha Power, who gets choked up with emotion as she explains how the closure of USAID is projected to result in more than 14 million preventable deaths. The film then cuts to heart-wrenching footage of families and children in Africa who have learned nutritional aid was being cut off. As the repercussions of Musk's actions are tallied, Gibney keeps coming back to the same question: How does his wealth keep growing despite it all? Lawrence Fossi, a longtime critic of Musk and Tesla, appears on screen to offer an explanation: investing in Musk's companies is not a bet on corporate America, "it's investing in a religion." This observation gets to the heart of Gibney's central argument about Musk: that he is a hype artist whose highest skill is making financiers and the public believe in him.  "His motives may have been pure at the beginning. But over time, in an attempt to get his companies to succeed, he ruthlessly broke the rules many of us live by. Musk is just the latest example of what I call noble cause corruption. Essentially, it's a belief that you're justified in breaking the rules because you think you are a force for good. Over time, as you begin to imagine you can get away with anything, the corruption becomes as total as the zealotry," Gibney said in promotional materials provided to the press. Ashley St. Clair, formerly a pro-Trump influencer who has turned against the MAGA movement, plays a major role in the film. She's Musk's ex and the mother of one of his children. In the film, St. Clair says one of the more outlandish and confounding claims Musk made to her was that he would "unleash the anomaly in the matrix" ahead of the 2024 presidential election to ensure Donald Trump would win. She said Musk texted her that he has "over 10 thousand lasers in space." (NPR obtained and authenticated the texts between Musk and St. Clair.)                  Ashley St. Clair, who was in a relationship with Musk and has a child with him, at the documentary's debut at the 83rd International Venice Film Festival on Sept. 8, 2026.                                                           Tiziana Fabi/AFP via Getty Images                                       hide caption  Gibney asked St. Clair if she understood this to be a reference to Musk's SpaceX. St. Clair replied, "I don't know where else he has lasers," before dwelling on the moment, as if to force the viewer to think hard about Musk's sci-fi gibberish. Election officials repeatedly debunked the false narrative purporting to show a connection between SpaceX's Starlink satellites and the November vote count. Nonetheless, the theory ricocheted online in the days after the 2024 election.  Musk's legal threat to Gibney seized on that moment with St. Clair, saying the film elevating a disproven theory is problematic. Musk's lawyer wrote that "the insinuation is false" and "the material refuting it is public." While most of Gibney's film is rooted in solid facts, he does dabble in conspiratorial thinking in the scene about the "lasers in space," and later in the film when he raises the specter of Musk using DOGE data to somehow interfere in the November midterms, another idea without any evidence.  Throughout the film, other Musk texts emerge.  After The Wall Street Journal published an article detailing Musk's alleged recreational drug use, which was raising concerns among leaders at SpaceX, St. Claire said Musk personally called News Corp. owner Rupert Murdoch in hopes he would intervene to stop the reporting. He did not. Musk then texted St. Clair that the Journal's articles were "saying that I'm high all the time." Musk added in a separate text: "I mean, I'm high a little … sure," punctuating the message with a shrugging emoji. NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. The systems that carry you to your first ten thousand customers are the same ones that quietly give out at a hundred thousand, and most teams don’t notice until the failure is already costing them money. By the time a payments company signs its hundred-thousandth customer, most of the founding team has quietly decided the hard part is over. Product-market fit is proven, the licenses are in place, the growth curve has started bending the right way. In my experience, that is almost exactly when things begin to break. Scaling a regulated payments business past six figures of customers is not a larger version of what got you to six thousand. It is a different job that happens to look the same from the outside. The shortcuts that worked so well early were built for a company that no longer exists, and the shift creeps up on you before anyone registers that the old problems have changed shape. Here are four I have watched catch nearly everyone. Every fast-growing company makes the same bet early. Ship now, fix later. It is usually the right bet. You do not build for a million users when you have a thousand, and the ones that pour their energy into scale they don’t have yet tend to run out of road before they ever need it. The trouble is that “later” shows up without warning. That workaround you wrote to launch a product in three weeks instead of three months? Still running two years on, undocumented, quietly load-bearing, and the one engineer who understood it left eight months ago. Volume finally drags it into the light. Reconciliation jobs that ran in minutes now take hours; a schema that made sense for one product now groans under six. Nothing crashes in a way that makes the news. It just degrades until your engineers spend more of the week holding the thing upright than building anything new. What actually helps: treat technical debt as a business risk with a number on it, not an engineering nuisance to apologize for. The teams that get through it pay down the load-bearing debt before the volume forces their hand. Waiting for the outage just makes the same repair cost more. Here is the one almost nobody warns you about, and it can sink you fastest. Every new market adds a layer: its own settlement cycle, banking partners, liquidity requirements and safeguarding rules. Anyone is manageable alone. Stack them across a dozen markets, and you have a system that needs constant coordination just to stay still. When you are small, moving money is a technical question. The transfer goes through, or it doesn’t. Scale across currencies and settlement timelines, and it becomes a live balancing act. You are holding client funds that must stay safeguarded and untouched, funding payouts into markets that settle on different schedules, carrying FX exposure that did not exist when everything sat in one currency, all while making sure the right account, in the right jurisdiction, always has enough to meet an obligation the moment it falls due. Get this wrong and you are not looking at a soft quarter. You are looking at a customer who cannot withdraw their own money, a safeguarding breach, a regulator asking questions you cannot answer cleanly. Treasury is where ordinary sloppiness can end the company. What actually helps: give the treasury a real seat at the table before the complexity lands, not after. Build the visibility and controls while the money flows are still simple enough for one person to hold in their head. Bolting rigor on afterwards is one of the hardest things a growing financial company will ever attempt. Early-stage culture runs on a particular fuel. Everyone knows more or less everything, decisions get made in a hallway on the way to lunch, and any competent person can reach into any part of the business and fix what needs fixing. That closeness is a genuine edge while it lasts, and it is impossible to carry past a certain headcount. Somewhere between fifty and a few hundred people, the informal system quietly stops working. The person who used to hold all the context now holds a slice of it. A call that once took two minutes now takes three meetings and still comes out worse. Too many things now, too few people who can see the whole board. What usually happens next is an overcorrection: approval chains, extra layers, documentation written mostly to feel documented. Companies lose the thing that made them quick and do not get the coordination they were reaching for in return. What actually helps: get explicit about what you are really selecting for, then defend it as you grow. At my company, the short list we do not compromise on is people who walk toward a hard problem instead of quietly managing their distance from it, who take initiative without waiting to be told, and who hold a standard that does not move when nobody is watching. Instincts like those do not scale on their own. You name them, hire them on purpose, and protect them, or growth waters them down without anyone deciding it should. At low volume, onboarding is deceptively cheap. A person reviews each application, spots the odd edge case, makes a call and moves on. The friction is real but invisible, absorbed by people who still have time in their day. At a hundred thousand clients, that process becomes a wall. Manual reviews that were a minor cost are now a queue that never empties. Edge cases that used to be rare arrive daily, because rare things happen constantly once the numbers are big enough. And onboarding is the first thing a customer experiences of you, so when it runs slow and is inconsistent, it becomes a leading cause of drop-off right after you have paid to acquire them. You cannot automate the problem away either. The rules around verifying who your customers are do not loosen as you grow. If anything, the scrutiny goes up with your size. What actually helps: build onboarding as a system that improves under volume rather than buckling, with automation handling the clear cases rigorously and human judgment saved for the genuinely ambiguous ones. The companies that treat it as core to the product, not a cost center to minimize, are the ones whose growth does not strangle itself at the front door. Any one of these, alone, is a problem you could solve on a normal Tuesday. The difficulty is that they do not arrive one at a time. They surface at roughly the same stage of growth, all leaning on the organization at once, which is why they are so easy to underestimate. They show up wearing the clothes of success: more customers, more volume, more markets. And they turn the very systems that got you here against you. The uncomfortable part of scaling a regulated financial business is that your early wins install your later problems. The reconciliation shortcut, the treasury flow held together by hand, the informal culture, the manual onboarding: everyone was the correct call on the day you made it, and everyone becomes a liability at scale because it worked so well, for so long, that nobody thought to question it. The teams that clear the wall are not the ones who dodged these traps. Nobody dodges them. They are the ones who saw the wall coming a stage early and started rebuilding while the old system was still standing. That, in the end, is the whole thing. Not avoiding the wall. Seeing it in time.  By the time a payments company signs its hundred-thousandth customer, most of the founding team has quietly decided the hard part is over. Product-market fit is proven, the licenses are in place, the growth curve has started bending the right way. In my experience, that is almost exactly when things begin to break. Scaling a regulated payments business past six figures of customers is not a larger version of what got you to six thousand. It is a different job that happens to look the same from the outside. The shortcuts that worked so well early were built for a company that no longer exists, and the shift creeps up on you before anyone registers that the old problems have changed shape. Here are four I have watched catch nearly everyone.
